en: The Sūtra on the Most Excellent Dharma-Gate of the Analysis of Dependent Origination, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
At the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery,
there was a great assembly of bhikṣus gathered together in the Hall of Comfort, sitting and engaging in this kind of mutual discussion,
saying: "Venerable sirs!..."
The Blessed One has, through countless diverse methods, taught the twelvefold profound dependent origination; therein, at the very beginning, he proclaimed ignorance as the causal condition.
For what reason, among all the conditions for afflictions and formative activities (*saṃskāra*), is only ignorance (*avidyā*) said to be their causal nature?
What excellence is seen in this ignorance?
Due to these causes and conditions, a dispute arose.
At that time, the World-Honored One, while dwelling in the celestial abodes, heard of this matter with his pure divine ear, which transcends that of humans.

In the evening, he rose from his meditative seclusion and proceeded to the Hall of Tranquility. There, before the great assembly, he arranged his seat as usual, sat down cross-legged, and with a clear and beautiful voice addressed the multitude:
"For what reason have you gathered in this hall to engage in contentious debate?"
"What is the subject of your discussion as you gather here now?
At that time, the great assembly addressed him, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
We have gathered here and engaged in this kind of mutual discussion, saying:
"Venerable sirs!

The Blessed One has previously, by means of countless diverse approaches, taught the twelvefold profound dependent origination; therein, at the very beginning, he proclaimed ignorance as the causal condition."
For what reason, among all the conditions consisting of afflictions and formative forces (*saṃskāra*), is ignorance alone designated as the causal nature?
What excellence is seen in this ignorance?
"World-Honored One!
It is because of these causes and conditions that we have given rise to this dispute; it is for the sake of discussing this matter that we have now gathered here in this assembly.
Having spoken these words, they ceased.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"I possess this sublime Dharma-gate of the analysis of dependent origination; you should listen attentively and apply your minds with thorough care, for I shall speak it for you."
What is called the "Dharma-gate of the Primary Excellence of the Analysis of Conditioned Arising"?
It refers to the teaching that, due to eleven kinds of distinguished matters, ignorance is proclaimed as the causal nature at the very beginning of conditioned arising.
What are these eleven? They are:

excellence of the object of focus (*ālambana*), excellence of the mode of activity (*ākāra*), excellence of the causal condition (*pratyaya*), excellence of the motivation (*samutthāna*), excellence of transformation (*anyathātva*), excellence of wrong practice (*mithyāpratipatti*), excellence of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), excellence of function (*karma*), excellence of obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), excellence of subsequent bondage (*anubandha*), and excellence of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
At that time, a certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in homage to the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What is the distinction regarding the objects of ignorance?
The Blessed One replied:

"The objects of ignorance are all categories of affliction—whether causes or effects—that possess various faults and defects, as well as all categories of purification—whether causes or effects—that possess various virtues and merits. This is called the distinction regarding the objects of ignorance."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
In what way is the characteristic of ignorance (avidyā) distinguished?"
The World-Honored One said:
"In this way, ignorance obscures reality and manifests falsehood as its characteristic mode of activity.
This is called the distinction of the characteristic mode of ignorance."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
what is the excellence of the causal condition of ignorance?”
The Blessed One said:
“In this way, ignorance serves as the causal condition, the root, and the basis for all defilements of afflictions, all defilements of karma, and all defilements of birth.”
What is the defilement of all afflictions?

Briefly stated, there are three categories of affliction that comprehensively encompass all defilements of affliction: namely, the affliction of ignorance, the affliction of doubt, and the affliction of perversion.
What are all the defilements of karma?

Briefly stated, they consist of three distinctions of intrinsic characteristics (the actions of body, speech, and mind) and three distinctions of remedies for obstacles (meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable karma), which collectively encompass all defilements of karma.
What are the defilements of all births?

Briefly stated, there are three types of suffering—namely, the suffering of change, the suffering of pain, and the suffering of conditioned formations—which arise based on the three feelings (pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure) and comprehensively encompass all the defilements of birth.
In what way does ignorance serve as the causal condition, the root, and the basis for all defilements of afflictions, all defilements of karma, and all defilements of birth?

This refers to two kinds of delusion regarding the truths, which cause all afflictive obscurations (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to increase and expand;
which cause all karmic obscurations (*karma-saṃkleśa*) that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to accumulate;
and which cause all birth-related obscurations (*janma-saṃkleśa*) that have not yet arisen to arise, and those already arisen to persist without turning back.

Therefore, I say that this ignorance serves as the causal condition, the root, and the basis for all defilements of afflictions, all defilements of karma, and all defilements of birth; this is called the excellence of the causal condition of ignorance.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
What is the excellence of the origination of ignorance?”
The Blessed One replied:

"This ignorance refers to either delusion regarding the future self-entity subsumed under the Truth of Suffering, or delusion regarding the present self-entity already obtained, which is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering. For such a deluded person, there may be the dependent origination of that which draws forth and that which is drawn forth, or the dependent origination of that which gives rise to and that which is given rise to."
"These two types of dependent origination take ignorance regarding the self-entity in future and present lives as their motivating condition.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
“What is the dependent origination of the projectors and the projected?
The Blessed One replied: “First, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations;

with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness; with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition there are the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition there is contact; with contact as condition there is feeling. This is called the dependent origination of the projectors and the projected.”
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
How is it that dependent origination gives rise to that which is produced?"

The Blessed One said: "The second [mode] is that ignorance conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging and death. This is called dependent origination as the producer and the produced."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘the first ignorance acting as the equal-arising condition for the dependent origination that is both the projector and the projected’?”
The Blessed One replied:
"It refers to a certain class of persons who, being deluded regarding the nature of their own selfhood in future existence, immediately give rise to a longing for that future existence."
Driven by the craving for future existence arising from ignorance, one perceives excellence in that future existence.
Furthermore, due to false conceptualization, one becomes attached to pleasant and unpleasant objects in the present life and thus performs non-meritorious actions.

Because they give rise to attachment toward their requisites, or because they give rise to hatred toward those they dislike, and because they fail to discern the merits and faults associated with these states due to negligence and folly, they commit such evil deeds.

Thus, regarding all faults pertaining to future lives, one is unable to reflect upon them nor comprehend their characteristics; in this way, ignorance serves as the condition for such non-meritorious formations.
If, regarding future existence, one perceives superior merit or perceives renunciation, one then performs meritorious actions or immovable actions.
Relying upon the teachings or instructions, because one initiates discernment and cultivation, one is able to perform such actions.

It should be understood that although such analytical cultivation occurs within a virtuous mind, it is nevertheless an improper mental attention; therefore, it is induced by ignorance regarding future existence. This is because one perceives superior qualities in future existence while being shrouded by ignorance, and because one perceives renunciation while being shrouded by ignorance.

In this way, non-meritorious, meritorious, and immovable formations—which serve as obstacles and their respective remedies—arise and perish simultaneously with the six groups of consciousness; they are able to deposit all formations within the resultant maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) that has already attained arising and ceasing in the present.
Through these skillful means, the three types of habitual tendencies (vāsanā) grasp the seeds for the production of a new existence.

Because they grasp the seeds for a new existence, name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), contact (sparśa), and sensation (vedanā)—which constitute the new existence—arise in succession within that future birth.

These factors, such as name-and-form, within the resultant consciousness already obtained in the present, possess only the nature of a cause and not yet the nature of a fruit; therefore, they are termed "projected dependent origination."
"This is called the first instance where ignorance acts as the condition for the origination of the dependent origination that is both the projector and the projected.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by 'the second ignorance acting as the condition for the simultaneous arising of its own production and that which is produced through dependent origination'?
The Blessed One replied:

"It refers to a certain class of persons who, being deluded regarding their presently acquired self-body, experience feelings conditioned by the six bases of contact, and thereby give rise to attachment."
Due to relishing [feeling], one yearns for such types of feeling in the future.
Due to this yearning, when one pursues them, grasping arises. With craving arising from pleasant feeling as its condition, the grasping of desire (*kāma-upādāna*) is produced.
What is called "desire-grasping" refers to the false discrimination and craving regarding various desires.
With this as the primary factor and this as the precursor, all afflictions of the desire realm come into being.

Furthermore, if one takes that painful feeling as a condition, there arises craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*), which is accompanied by aversion and detachment, induced by what is unreasonable, and associated with aversion and detachment. When, relying on this craving, one seeks non-existence through improper means, one immediately gives rise to the evil view of renunciation (*naiṣkramyadṛṣṭi*), the evil view of fixed periodicity (*kāladṛṣṭi*), and the evil views upon which these two depend.
For this reason, it is called "clinging conditioned by craving.

If one dies while relying on this very clinging and without being separated from desire and lust, then by virtue of these views and all the afflictions of the desire realm, it is called "clinging conditioned by craving for the desire realm."
If one is free from sensual desire, or free from desire for the realm of form, then craving for the realm of form or craving for the formless realm finds a place to arise.

When those afflictions operate within the realm of form or the formless realm, they give rise to grasping for the realm of form or the formless realm; thus, these various afflictions of form and the formless, along with their respective views, are called "grasping conditioned by craving for the realm of form" and "grasping conditioned by craving for the formless realm."

With craving as a condition, that [consciousness] takes up grasping; the previously obtained ripening-result consciousness, which has been perfumed by various formations, is called "possessing grasping.

Sustained by such grasping, the seeds of formations and so forth previously accumulated manifest their functional capacity in this or that place whenever craving for those respective places has not been severed, thereby giving rise to future existence.

Because those formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are capable of bringing about future birth and cause the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*) to enter the present, they are called "existence" (*bhava*).
Through the power of grasping (*upādāna*), these formations and so forth become existence.
With this as the condition, when one passes away from this life, that which was previously projected gradually arises; for this reason, it is called "conditioned by existence, there is birth.

Once birth has occurred, the transformation of the temporal phases that first arose is called aging, and the exhaustion of the life-force at the very end is called death; therefore, it is said that "conditioned by birth, there is aging and death."
"This is called the second instance where ignorance serves as the condition of origination for its own producer and that which is produced by it within dependent origination.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason do you not say that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*)—these two types of productive conditions—are the conditions for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)?
The Blessed One replied:
"Because craving and grasping have their own respective domains and are limited in scope."

Why is this so? It is because it is not logical for craving and grasping of the desire realm to serve as the condition for the arising of those immovable formations belonging to the form or formless realms, as they do not constitute its objective sphere.

Just as it is said that the two types of craving and grasping in the desire realm [contribute] to immovable formations, so too should one understand that the two types of craving and grasping in the form realm [contribute] to the immovable formations of the formless realm; and that the two types of craving and grasping in the formless realm [contribute] to formations of the desire realm or the form realm, as well as the two types of craving and grasping in the form realm [contributing] to formations of the desire realm, are likewise to be understood.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason do the two types of craving and grasping in the desire realm not serve as conditions for non-meritorious and meritorious formations?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"Because of the predominant power of various present objects that are either desirable or undesirable, one gives rise to sensual craving, produces unwholesome roots, and performs non-meritorious actions; all of this is due to not knowing the faults within the causes and effects of those non-meritorious actions."
Because his intention (āśaya) is flawed, or because his application (prayoga) is flawed, he gives rise to non-meritorious action (apuṇya-karman).
Such flaws in intention and application have ignorance (avidyā) alone as their predominant condition, rather than craving for objects (viṣaya-tṛṣṇā) or the unwholesome roots (akuśala-mūla).

If one performs various meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*) out of sensual craving (*kāmarāga*), it is because that craving relies upon faith to perform such actions, for it gives rise to firm conviction regarding death and rebirth.
Since this craving and grasping (*upādāna*) are subdued by faith, I designate them as "obscured-unspecified" (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).

If a dharma of the desire realm is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), it lacks superior efficacy in initiating the various formations (*saṃskāra*). This is because, regarding cause and effect as well as meritorious formations (*puṇyasaṃskāra*), such a dharma does not know the way of transcendence; rather, seeking a desirable rebirth, one performs these meritorious formations. Thus, even this meritorious formation has only ignorance as its predominant condition.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do craving and grasping pertaining to the form realm not act as conditions for the imperturbable formations of the form realm?”
The World-Honored One replied:
"For those who have not yet abandoned craving for the desire realm, the craving for the form realm and so forth has not yet found a place of arising.
If there is no place of arising, there is no capacity [for such action]; therefore, it is not the condition for immovable karma of the form realm."
Just as it is said that the two types of craving and grasping for the realm of form [give rise to] the various immovable formations of the realm of form,
so too should it be understood that the two types of craving and grasping for the formless realm [give rise to] the various immovable formations of the formless realm.

Regarding that body which possesses defects within the realm of form or the formless realm, one gives rise to the perception and view that it possesses virtuous qualities. Whether relying on the Dharma of teaching or the Dharma of instruction, one initiates such improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), which serves as the condition for the formations of immovability (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*) in those realms.

Thus, the improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) that arises is induced by ignorance; this ignorance, accompanied by the improper mental attention thus produced and its fruit, can serve as the condition for the formless realm formations (*ārūpyadhātu-aniñjya-saṃskāra*).
Therefore, it should be understood that even those immovable formations (*āniñjya-saṃskāra*) have only ignorance as their predominant condition.

Furthermore, there is a class of beings who, relying on the craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*), perform various meritorious or immovable formations; since they perceive many faults in all states of existence (*bhava*) due to such craving for non-existence, how could they ever again long for future existences?
However, because one does not know non-existence as it truly is, due to this ignorance, one fails to attain the true path of remedy for existence.
Furthermore, due to this ignorance, one conceives the notion of a remedy regarding what is not a remedy, thereby performing various meritorious actions or imperturbable actions.
"By this reasoning, it should be understood that these formations have only ignorance as their condition, and not craving or grasping as the conditions for the formations.
He further said,
"World-Honored One!"

“Regarding all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) that are associated with and co-existent with the six groups of consciousness, arising and ceasing together with them—by what reason is it said that formations are the condition for consciousness?
The Blessed One replied:

“Because the six groups of consciousness are associated with and co-existent with meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations, arising and ceasing together with them, they deposit the perfumed seeds of all formations within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), thereby projecting a new and distinct ripening consciousness for a future birth.”
By this principle, it is therefore declared that formations are the condition for consciousness.
He further said,
“World-Honored One!

For what reason are the seeds of the various factors—name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—simultaneously induced within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), yet are further said to occur in a sequence of priority and posteriority?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Because they arise in successive order in the future, it is spoken of in this way.
He further said:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason are name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling said to be the signs of the body to be born in the future?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Because it is the basis for the enjoyment of those causes, and because it is the substance of the enjoyment of those causes.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"If there were only names arising and no form at all, what fault would there be?
The World-Honored One replied,
"If during the course of a lifetime there were only names and they did not abide in dependence upon form, their continuous arising would be unreasonable."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
If there were only the arising of form and no name at all for it, what fault would there be?"
The World-Honored One said:
"If there were only form without the grasping of names, it would necessarily disintegrate and could not grow.
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
If one were to say only that consciousness conditions the six sense bases, what fault would there be?
The World-Honored One replied:

"At the time of initial birth, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are not yet complete; only the body faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the mind faculty (*manendriya*) are active. Therefore, it should be impossible for [the life-faculty] to have these two faculties as its substance."

Because name-and-form first exists, it gradually increases; since it serves as the condition for the subsequent fulfillment of the six sense bases, it is said that name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
If the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are fulfilled and the physical body is perfected, for what reason do you further speak of the two kinds of contact (sparśa) and sensation (vedanā)?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"If the six sense bases of the physical body are fully developed, although this constitutes the ultimate basis for experience, it cannot yet be called the 'ultimate experience. It is only through the presence of both causes and actual reception that one can be said to have attained the ultimate experience."

Therefore, one should know that it is only when both the ultimate basis for experience and the ultimate essence of the cause of experience are perfected that one can be said to have attained the perfection of the birth-body (*janmakāya*).
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
You have said that ignorance is the condition for the arising of craving, yet you have also said that feeling is the condition for craving."
“If it were the case that ignorance alone is the condition for craving, and not feeling, what fault would there be?
The World-Honored One replied:

“There are three kinds of craving; they ought to arise simultaneously. However, because craving depends upon feeling as its condition, they do not arise at one and the same time. By this principle, it is not the case that ignorance alone serves as the condition for craving.”
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
If that is so, and this craving has only feeling as its condition, what fault would there be in this?”
The World-Honored One replied:

"While it is true that all feelings (vedanā) have craving (tṛṣṇā) as their condition, there are nevertheless feelings that are not conditions for craving; these can serve as the condition for the total cessation of all cravings. Therefore, feeling alone is not the sole condition for craving."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
If it were taught that craving alone serves as the condition for becoming, without depending on grasping, what fault would there be in this?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"Longing is called craving; there is no longing for the perilous and evil realms. Nevertheless, because of non-meritorious actions performed, although one seeks a fortunate realm, a contrary result arises. When that result arises, could it possibly be conditioned by craving?"
One should simply apply that grasping as its condition.
Furthermore, as it has been said regarding those who lack craving for existence, they long for non-existence;
yet when seeking non-existence, because of their performance of meritorious and immovable karmic formations, a contrary result arises.
When this fruit arises, how could it be conditioned by craving?
One should state only that grasping (*upādāna*) is its condition.
By this principle, it is not the case that craving alone serves as the condition for becoming (*bhava*).
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
If grasping conditions existence (*bhava*), and existence conditions birth (*jāti*), for what reason do you not teach grasping and existence together as the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"Because craving can produce four kinds of karma: first, this craving, within the experience of its own objective sphere, performs the karma of binding through attachment to flavor;
second, this craving performs the karma of initiating the various types of grasping."
Third, this craving functions to bring about the karma of existence (*bhava*) that causes the previously projected formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to become actualized;
fourth, this craving functions as the karma that links death to subsequent rebirth.
"For this reason and by these conditions, craving alone is taught as the Truth of Origination.
He further said, "World-Honored One!

If birth, old age, and death have name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling as their characteristics, for what reason is the designation 'birth, old age, and death' applied specifically to this present body?"
The World-Honored One said:
"It is to manifest the characteristics of such a birth-body that there are three kinds of suffering which constitute its nature of suffering.
He further said:
“World-Honored One,
what suffering does birth manifest?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Birth reveals the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā).
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
"What suffering does old age manifest?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Old age manifests the suffering of decay."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
What suffering does death manifest?"
The World-Honored One said:
"Death manifests as the suffering of suffering.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these four kinds of characteristics of the birth-body, what are the differences arising from birth, old age, and death?
The World-Honored One replied:

"One should know that these four characteristics of the birth-body—whether arising in succession, whether belonging to that birth, or whether arising in such a manner—are called the characteristics of the birth of the birth-body."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
What is the sequence by which the birth-characteristic (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*) arises from the body of birth?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"First there is birth from planting the seed; immediately following that, there is birth by gradual growth; immediately following that, there is birth from the womb; and immediately following that, there is birth by gradual maturation."
"Once they have grown, through the experience of verbal expression they are able to attain equal birth; such categories as these are called 'sequential arising.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"To whom does this birth belong?
The Blessed One replied,
"In the arising of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, there is absolutely no self."
Why is this so? Because the aggregates and so forth increase gradually, their nature is impermanent; thus, for phenomena that are impermanent, there exists this characteristic of arising.
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
How does it arise?
The World-Honored One replied:

"By the power of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), there is a temporary abiding; because it is a phenomenon with a limited duration, its nature is impermanent, and thus impermanent phenomena arise in this manner.

One should know that these four characteristics of the produced body, as they undergo transformation over time, are capable of effecting five kinds of deterioration, which is termed 'aging' (*jarā*)."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
What are called the five kinds of decline?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"First, the beard and hair undergo decay, because their color has become withered and ruined;
second, the physical characteristics undergo decay, because the complexion, skin, and strength have all deteriorated."

Third is the decline of activity: when speaking, the breath rises and gasping becomes more urgent; because the body trembles, one stands hunched over as the waist and spine have lost all strength; because the body is frail and weak, one sits with the torso bent low; because the body is exhausted and debilitated, one must lean on a staff when walking; and because the intellect is dull and the mind is clouded, whatever one contemplates is characterized by ignorance and confusion. Fourth is the decline of enjoyment:

because the enjoyment of present resources is diminished, and because one is entirely unable to enjoy objects of play and pleasure in the present; because regarding the objects within the range of the various sense faculties, one cannot engage with them swiftly or clearly, or may not engage with them at all.
Fifth is the decline of the life-faculty: as the lifespan is nearing its end and death is imminent, even encountering minor conditions for death, one is unable to endure them.
Within these four types of birth and their physical characteristics, there are furthermore six kinds of distinctions regarding death:

first, ultimate death; second, non-ultimate death; third, death according to its own characteristic; fourth, the distinction of the portion of non-ultimate death; fifth, the distinction of the portion of ultimate death; and sixth, timely and untimely death.

It should be understood that herein, "death by its own characteristic" refers to the specific characteristic of consciousness departing from the body and the cessation and disappearance of the characteristic of form; thus, within the characteristics of the produced body, the characteristics of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth undergo differentiation through birth, aging, and death.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
Within dependent origination, you have spoken of three kinds of craving; all of these are conditions for the arising of the body."
"For what reason is it that, in many instances, only the birth-body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is mentioned?
The World-Honored One replied:

"Because the characteristics of the birth-body in the desire realm are the coarsest, because they are easily manifested, and because it is not a path from which one has attained permanent liberation or from which there is no falling back."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!

Regarding the various projecting dependent originations and the various producing dependent originations previously described, which consist of twelve members, among these members, how many are the projectors?"
How many are the induced?
How many are the productive?
How many are the produced?
The World-Honored One said:
"It should be known that among these twelve links, ignorance, formations, and one portion of consciousness are called the 'projecting factors' (ākṣepaka);
furthermore, another portion of consciousness, along with name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling, are called the 'projected factors' (ākṣipta)."
Furthermore, a portion of feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) is called "that which produces";

birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are called "that which is produced. It should be understood that a portion of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) are likewise called "that which is produced."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding these various factors, whether they are drawn forth or produced, do they arise simultaneously?”
"Do they arise sequentially?
The World-Honored One replied, "They arise simultaneously; they are taught in sequence."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
If these various factors arise simultaneously, for what reason do you first speak of their 'leading' (*ākṣepa*) and subsequently speak of their 'arising' (*utpāda*)?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"It is because there is that which leads to future existence that birth occurs; it is not because there is no such leading that it occurs.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Since ignorance also has improper mental attention as its condition, why do you speak of ignorance alone as the condition?
The World-Honored One replied:

"Furthermore, ignorance also induces improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra) as a condition for volitional formations (saṃskāra); moreover, craving arises conditioned by contact and feeling born from ignorance. For these reasons, it is specifically mentioned."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
Briefly, through how many aspects should dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) be understood?"
The Blessed One said:
“In brief, dependent origination should be understood through three characteristics:
first, by way of being devoid of agency; second, by way of the impermanence of its nature; and third, by way of its functional capacity.”
The Sūtra on the Analysis of the Primary Dharmas of the Arising of Conditions, Volume Upper;
The Sūtra on the Analysis of the Primary Dharmas of the Arising of Conditions, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree.
"Furthermore, World-Honored One! As stated elsewhere, there are four kinds of conditions:

namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)."
“World-Honored One!
By what conditions do you now say that ignorance conditions volitional formations? By what conditions do you say that the sequence continues down to birth conditioning aging and death?
The World-Honored One replied:

"I have taught based on the general characteristics of all conditioned phenomena that there are four kinds of conditions. However, in this present context, I speak only in terms of the single predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): that ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on in succession until birth conditions aging and death."
"This dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya) is further of two kinds: first, the distant; second, the proximate.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"In what way is this dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) distant?
In what way is it near?
The Blessed One replied:

"When improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) has not yet arisen, the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) acts as a remote predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
once it has arisen, it acts as an immediate predominant condition."
The formations induced by improper mental attention arise and cease simultaneously with the six groups of consciousness;
when they have not yet arisen, they serve as the remote dominant condition for consciousness, and once they have arisen, they serve as the proximate dominant condition for consciousness.
Before death and passing away, consciousness serves as the remote predominant condition for name-and-form;
once death and passing away have occurred, consciousness serves as the immediate predominant condition for name-and-form.
Just as consciousness is related to that name-and-form, so too is the name-and-form it has projected related to the name-and-form that arises from it.

Just as name-and-form is related to that name-and-form, so too are the six sense bases related to those six sense bases; and the same applies to contact in relation to contact, and feeling in relation to feeling.

Just as ignorance is related to those volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), so it is with ignorance in relation to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), craving in relation to grasping (*upādāna*), and grasping in relation to becoming (*bhava*).

Just as consciousness (*vijñāna*) is related to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and as name-and-form and the other factors are related to name-and-form and the others, so too is becoming related to birth (*jāti*).
If one is in the stages of the womb, infancy, childhood, or youth, birth acts as a remote dominant condition for aging and death;
when the faculties have matured and life is about to end, it should be understood that birth acts as a proximate dominant condition.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Since there are causes, conditions, and reasons for this, what is the underlying intention behind the teaching in the sūtras that craving is the cause of karma?”
The Blessed One replied:
"That there is an appropriating karmic activity which has craving as its cause—this is the intended meaning (saṃdhāya) spoken of herein.
He further said:
“Bhagavān, how should these three distinct meanings of cause (*hetu*), condition (*pratyaya*), and source (*nidāna*) be understood?
The Bhagavān replied:
"The sense of 'cause' (hetu) refers to the seeds capable of producing a subsequent birth;
the sense of 'condition' (pratyaya) refers to acting as the support and sustenance for this life so that it may arise;
and the sense of 'source' (yoni) refers to guiding toward and bringing about the immediate arising once life has ended."
"In this way, one should understand the distinctions between these three meanings.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the meaning of the term 'dependent origination' (pratītyasamutpāda)?
The Blessed One replied:

"In this way, these various factors each arise through the continuous succession of their respective conditions, combining without deficiency; such is the meaning of the term 'dependent origination'."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Is there only this dependent origination of the continuity of birth?”
"Is there yet another dependent origination distinct from this?
The Blessed One replied:
"The dependent origination I teach consists, in brief, of eight gates."

First, there is the teaching on the dependent origination of the enjoyment of conventional objects: that is, conditioned by the eye and visible forms, visual consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors constitutes contact; with contact as condition, sensation arises—and so it is explained in detail.
Second, there is the teaching on the dependent origination of maintenance: that is, conditioned by the four nutriments, the sense faculties and the primary elements abide and increase.

Third, there is the teaching on the dependent origination of the causes of nutriment: that is, seeking various grains, where the conditions of field, seed, and water give rise to sprouts and so forth.

Fourth, it is taught that there is the dependent origination of the continuity of all birth-bodies (*janma-kāya*), meaning that by means of the projecting [karma] (*ākṣepaka*), various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) are produced, which in turn give rise to all that is projected and produced.

Fifth, it is taught that there is the dependent origination of the support for all birth-bodies, meaning that all worlds are established through causes and conditions as undergoing formation and destruction.

Sixth, it is taught that there is the dependent origination of the differentiation of all birth-bodies, meaning that by means of unwholesome and wholesome contaminated karma (*sāsrava-karman*), the distinctions between the three evil destinies and the human and celestial realms are established.

Seventh, it is taught that there is a pure dependent origination (*pariśuddha-pratītyasamutpāda*): namely, by relying on the voices of others and by relying on one’s own internal appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), right view is produced, which is capable of extinguishing ignorance; because ignorance is extinguished, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are accordingly extinguished, and so on in detail until: because birth is extinguished, old age and death are accordingly extinguished.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Just as ignorance and the others arise in succession as conditions for volitional formations and so forth, do they likewise cease in that same succession?”
The Buddha said,
"It is not so. He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason do you teach their cessation in this sequential order?
The World-Honored One replied:

"It is for the purpose of demonstrating that by means of the non-arising capacity of the preceding members, the subsequent members are rendered subject to the state of non-arising; therefore, they are explained in succession. However, this does not mean that there is no sequential progression for the characteristic of arising or for phenomena subject to cessation."

Eighth, it is taught that there is dependent origination through mastery: that is to say, by taking well-cultivated meditative concentration as a condition, those who practice concentration achieve whatever they aspire to or delight in, all of which is accomplished without any difference in the end.
"This is what I have called the eightfold gateway of dependent origination, briefly explained by me.
He further said,
"World-Honored One!"
“As the Buddha has taught, birth arises because of karma and proceeds because of craving.
With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) was this said?
The Blessed One replied:

With ignorance as a condition, one previously, within the various realms of existence, performed and increased various meritorious, non-meritorious, or imperturbable formations, thereby projecting and appropriating the distinct seeds of various types of birth-bodies.
Within this existence, if craving has not been severed, then by means of that craving, it can cause the formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to evolve into that existence.
Existence possesses the functional capacity to give rise to the self-substance of a future existence; such a functional capacity is not separate from craving.
"It is with this underlying intention that it was said: 'Birth is caused by karma; rebirth is driven by craving.
He further asked:
"World-Honored One!"

“If the Blessed One says that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the cause of rebirth, for what reason do you say only grasping (*upādāna*) is the condition for existence (*bhava*), rather than saying craving is the condition for existence?
The Blessed One replied:

“If one is separated from grasping, craving alone cannot act as a condition to transform non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*) and so forth, thereby bringing about the link of existence (*bhavāṅga*) and causing birth in the evil destinies.”

Furthermore, if grasping were absent, the various forms of craving for existence could not serve as conditions to transform meritorious and immovable formations, thereby producing the link of becoming within both the non-concentrated and concentrated states, leading to rebirth in the various happy realms.
"Therefore, it is not only craving that serves as a condition for existence; rather, that branch of existence (bhava) definitely has grasping (upādāna) as its condition.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
As stated in the *Mahānidāna-paryāya-sūtra*: "O Ānanda!
If among those various classes of sentient beings there were no one born, then such and such types of birth would not exist."
"If all birth were entirely non-existent, one would not designate 'birth as the condition for old age and death.
With what underlying intention (saṃdhāya) was this said?
The Blessed One replied:

"This was spoken with two kinds of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): based on that which is produced by what has been drawn forth, and based on that which is produced by what has been produced.

Furthermore, it was spoken with two kinds of intentional meaning: based on old age and death as a remote dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), and based on old age and death as an immediate dominant condition."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!

You have previously given a brief explanation of the meaning of the phrases regarding dependent origination, yet the actual meaning of dependent origination has not yet been explained. How should it be understood?”

The Blessed One said: "In brief, there are eleven meanings of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) that should be understood as follows: the meaning of 'absence of an agent' is the meaning of dependent origination; the meaning of 'arising from causes' is the meaning of dependent origination;

the meaning of 'freedom from a sentient being' is the meaning of dependent origination; the meaning of 'arising in dependence on others' is the meaning of dependent origination; the meaning of 'absence of activity' is the meaning of dependent origination; the meaning of 'the impermanence of nature' is the meaning of dependent origination; the meaning of 'momentary destruction' is the meaning of dependent origination; the meaning of 'the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect' is the meaning of dependent origination; the meaning of 'the differentiation of various classes of causes and effects' is the meaning of dependent origination; the meaning of 'the mutual conformity between cause and effect' is the meaning of dependent origination; and the meaning of 'the certainty and non-confusion of cause and effect' is the meaning of dependent origination."
"In this way, one should understand the brief meaning of dependent origination.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
"As stated in other sūtras, dependent origination is profound.
How should one understand the characteristics of such profundity in dependent origination?
The Blessed One replied:
"Based on the brief meaning of the eleven links of dependent origination, one should understand the five profound characteristics of dependent origination.
What are these five? First, the profundity of cause;
second, the profundity of characteristic; third, the profundity of arising; fourth, the profundity of differentiation; and fifth, the profundity of transmigration."
One should know that the characteristics of the profound nature of dependent origination are further fivefold.
What are these five? They are: the profundity of its characteristics;

the profundity of the various members of the causal sequence of production; the profundity of the various members of the causal sequence of arising; the profundity of its distinctions; and the profundity of its remedies.
One should know that dependent origination further possesses five kinds of profound characteristics.
What are these five? They are:
the profundity of inclusion, the profundity of forward order, the profundity of reverse order, the profundity of grasping, and the profundity of the sphere of activity.
"This is called the excellence of the origination of ignorance.
He further said,
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the distinction regarding the transformation of ignorance?
The Blessed One replied,
"Briefly stated, there are four kinds of transformation of ignorance."
What are the four?

First, the transformation of latent tendencies (anuśaya); second, the transformation of active fetters (paryavasthāna); third, the transformation of association (saṃprayoga); and fourth, the transformation of the unique (asādhāraṇa).
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
What kind of transformation does ignorance undergo, such that you say ignorance is the condition for the arising of volitional formations?"
The Blessed One replied:

"External phenomena consist of the four types of transformation induced by improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra) in ordinary beings; with these as conditions, there arise meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable formations (saṃskāras)."

Thus, it is said that all wholesome minds associated with the meritorious and immovable formations of ordinary beings regarding external phenomena are outflows induced by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).

Regarding internal phenomena, if an ordinary person is heedless, with the exception of one type of non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), the remaining types of ignorance induce heedlessness; conditioned by this, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise.

Regarding internal phenomena, if ordinary beings who are diligent in practice without negligence, as well as noble learners (*śaikṣa*), give rise to deluded thoughts through the three types of ignorance, these serve as conditions for non-merit; however, this non-merit cannot act as a condition to summon rebirth in the three evil destinies.
Therefore, this is non-merit; I do not say that it is formations conditioned by ignorance.

Regarding this aforementioned unshared ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), although ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who practice the internal teachings may be diligent and not negligent, those in training (*śaikṣa*) have not yet been able to abandon it; it should be known that the noble ones in training (*ārya-śaikṣa*) have permanently abandoned it.

Furthermore, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is not negligent practices internal dharmas—whether performing meritorious formations (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*) or immovable formations (*āniñjyābhisaṃskāra*)—these are induced by a virtuous mind associated with correct mental attention (*yoniso-manasikāra*) toward the True Dharma. Because they are induced by taking liberation as their basis and dedicating [the merit] toward liberation, although they result in a distinguished birth within the happy realms (*sugati*), ignorance does not act as a predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for them; nevertheless, it can still function as those four types of ignorance.

Because the noble learners (*śaikṣa*) who have severed the dominant condition have forever abandoned the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*), they do not create new karma. Although all previously accumulated karma has not yet been permanently extinguished due to the power of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they merely touch it and then reject it. Thus, all formations conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*) gradually diminish with each birth and no longer increase.

By this principle, it should be understood that those within the internal Dharma who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) do not, due to ignorance (*avidyā*), further create formative forces (*saṃskāra*).

Therefore, I declare that the sequential dependent origination of defilement (*saṃkleśa-pratītyasamutpāda*) is most perfectly complete only in relation to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) based on external phenomena, and not for those abiding in the internal Dharma; this is called the excellence of the transformation of ignorance.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
What is the distinction regarding ignorance and wrong conduct?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"Those four types of ignorance are all capable of giving rise to two kinds of false practices—namely, superimposition and denial—regarding the various truths."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
What are called the two kinds of wrong practices: superimposition and denial?”
The World-Honored One replied:

"Due to the four inversions—namely, viewing what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, or viewing what is the Dharma as not the Dharma; or viewing that which is not a means for rebirth in heaven or the path to liberation as a means, and viewing that which is a means as not a means—these are called the superimposition of wrong practice.
All forms of disparagement and all false views are called the denial of wrong practice."
"This is called the excellence of the wrong practice of ignorance.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"What are the distinctive characteristics of ignorance?
The World-Honored One replied:
"One should know that ignorance has two kinds of characteristics:"

First is the excellence of its subtle specific characteristic; second is the excellence of its pervasive general characteristic regarding objects that are pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. Why is this so?
Even the *paryavasthāna* (active manifestation) of ignorance is subtle, difficult to know, and difficult to comprehend; how much more so is the *anuśaya* (latent tendency) of ignorance?

Even the associated ignorance is subtle, difficult to know, and difficult to comprehend; how much more so is the unique (*āveṇika*) ignorance that pervades all desirable, undesirable, and neutral objects, obscuring the true nature (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), manifesting false appearances (*abhūta-nimitta*), and functioning through common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
No other afflictions possess such characteristics; therefore, it is preeminent.

Other common-characteristic afflictions, such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, also arise by depending upon ignorance (*avidyā*); this is called the preeminence of the characteristics of ignorance.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
In what way is the activity of ignorance particularly distinguished?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"One should know that ignorance has, in brief, two kinds of functional activities:
first, ignorance universally functions as the basis for all cyclic existence; second, ignorance universally functions as an obstacle to all states of quiescence."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
What is called ‘all transmigration’?”
The Blessed One replied:

"Whether it revolves in this place, whether it revolves as this object, or whether it revolves in such a manner, I categorically describe all of these as 'all-encompassing transmigration' (sarva-saṃsāra)."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Where does this turn?”
The World-Honored One replied,
"It is through my discernment regarding the three periods of time.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
what is it that revolves?
The World-Honored One replied:
"The six internal and external bases arise from grasping at a self.
He further said,
"World-Honored One!"
"How does it proceed?
The World-Honored One replied,
"The continuity of the maturation of various karmas proceeds by means of self-conceptualization and false conceptualization."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One,
what is meant by 'the complete cessation of all things'?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"In brief, there are four kinds of complete stillness (*śamatha*):

first, the basis of stillness; second, the object of stillness; third, the mental attention of stillness; and fourth, the accomplishment of the fruit of stillness. These are called the distinctions in the functioning of ignorance."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
In what way does ignorance constitute an obstacle to excellence?"
The Blessed One said:
"One should know that ignorance obstructs the supreme Dharma and obstructs the vast Dharma.
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
How does ignorance obstruct the supreme Dharma?
The World-Honored One replied:

"As for what is called 'the supreme dharma,' it is that which can gather the five faculties and cause them to harmonize; this is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). That which obstructs this is ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, it is called 'obstructing the supreme dharma.'"
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One,
how does ignorance obstruct the vast Dharma?"
The World-Honored One replied:

"What is called the 'vast Dharma' refers to the wisdom born of hearing, the wisdom born of reflection, and the wisdom born of cultivation. That which obstructs these is ignorance; therefore, it is called the obstruction to the vast Dharma."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
As it is said that the absence of wisdom is called ignorance (*avidyā*), does this mean that merely the absence of wisdom is what is termed ignorance?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"It is not merely that the absence of knowledge is ignorance.
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
If it were merely that wisdom is absent which constitutes ignorance, what fault would there be?
The World-Honored One replied:
"If that were so, it would be impossible to establish a definitive essential characteristic for ignorance. Why is this?
Because within the essence of knowledge derived from hearing, there is no knowledge derived from reflection."
Within the substance of the wisdom produced by reflection, there is no wisdom produced by cultivation;
within the substance of all mundane wisdom produced by cultivation, there is no supramundane wisdom produced by cultivation;
and within the supramundane wisdom of those still in training (śaikṣa), there is no wisdom of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Above the wisdom of a śrāvaka who has nothing further to learn (aśaikṣa), there is no such thing as the Tathāgata’s equalizing wisdom (samatājñāna).
If this were the case, then wisdom would be identical to non-wisdom; likewise, it would be impossible to establish a definitive essential nature for ignorance (avidyā).

Furthermore, regarding those three wholesome roots, I have stated that there is "non-delusion" (amoha). It should be understood that while "delusion" (moha) itself is absent, it is not the mere absence of delusion that is called non-delusion; rather, it is not the case that the absence of "clarity" (vidyā) is called ignorance (avidyā). Instead, there is a distinct mental factor (caitta-dharma) which, because it does not know reality as it truly is, is designated as ignorance.

If it were the case that there exists a distinct mental factor (*caitasika*) which, by cognizing reality, is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*), and that "ignorance" (*avidyā*) is merely the absence of such clarity, then there would be no such eleven specific types of ignorance.
"Therefore, it should be understood that ignorance is not merely the absence of knowledge; this is what is called the 'superiority of the obstruction of ignorance.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the excellence of the latent bondage of ignorance?
The Blessed One replied:

"As far as sentient beings in the three realms up to the Peak of Existence, they possess the latent tendencies of non-knowledge regarding the Truths; because these are neither deficient nor diminished, those sentient beings are said to be 'fully bound'."

Furthermore, regarding this ignorance, there is a distinction between the causes and effects of the happy and miserable realms: sentient beings in the formless realm possess the inferior grade, sentient beings in the form realm possess the middling grade, and sentient beings in the desire realm possess the superior grade; thus, they accomplish these three grades of nescience.
Among all classes of sentient beings who are to be born in the future, each is naturally bound by three grades [of defilements].

This refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); as for the noble ones (*ārya*), they gradually and permanently sever them—some possess the upper and middle grades while having the middle and lower, or some possess the middle and lower grades while lacking the upper and middle.

Furthermore, although Arhats have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and are liberated from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one should know that they still possess the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which comprises the latent bondage of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*). This ignorance should be understood to follow sentient beings for an extremely long time; with the exception of the Buddhas, all others remain bound by it.
"This is called the excellence of the binding by the accompaniment of ignorance.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is the excellence of the antidote to ignorance?
The Blessed One replied,
"There are two sublime knowledges that serve as the antidote to ignorance."
What are these two?
First, relying on the voices of others, or the subtle wisdom of the partially limited dharma-realm;
second, relying on the voices of others, the subtle wisdom of the entirely limitless dharma-realm.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
with what as its object does the subtle wisdom of the partially limited dharma-realm take its support?”
"What are their modes of activity?
What are their undertakings?
The World-Honored One replied:

The subtle, limited, and measureable wisdom of the dharma-realm takes the sixteen aspects of the four noble truths as its object, performing the work of severing the bonds of all defilements—such as ignorance and other afflictions—that give rise to all forms of impurity.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
How should one understand the characteristics of the suffering of birth?"
The Blessed One replied:

“It is because it is the nature of being the basis for suffering conditioned by internal factors; it is because it is the nature of being the basis for suffering conditioned by external factors; and it is because it is the nature of being the basis for suffering conditioned by both.”
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics of that which is internally conditioned by suffering?"
The World-Honored One replied,
"They are the suffering of illness, the suffering of old age, and the suffering of death.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
what are the characteristics of suffering that has external conditions?
The World-Honored One replied:
“Suffering from union with the unloved, suffering from separation from the loved, and suffering from not obtaining what one seeks.
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
"What are the characteristics of that which takes suffering as its object?
The Blessed One replied:
"Briefly stated, it is the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One,
what is meant by 'craving'?"
The Blessed One replied:
"It refers to attachment to one's own self in the present.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
What are the characteristics of craving for future existence?
The World-Honored One replied:
"It refers to the longing for one's own self-existence in the future.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is craving that proceeds together with delight and greed?
The World-Honored One replied,
"It refers to the deep attachment and relishing toward acquired and possessed material wealth and manifest sensory objects."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
What is meant by 'delightful craving for this and that'?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"It refers to the various pursuits for the acquisition of wealth and resources that have not yet been obtained and do not currently lie within one's field of experience.
He further said:
“World-Honored One,
how is this craving completely severed so that nothing remains?
The World-Honored One replied:

“Because the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing and cultivation have been severed; because the fetters of the lower and upper realms have been severed; because they have been severed forever; because craving for future results of suffering has been severed; and because craving for present results of suffering has been severed—this is called the complete and permanent abandonment of this craving without remainder.”
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
How does one relinquish?”
The World-Honored One replied,
"Because the afflictions to be abandoned through insight have been severed.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘transforming and vomiting’?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Because the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have been severed.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"How is it that they are eternally exhausted?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Because all the lower fetters have been permanently severed."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
How does one practice detachment?”
The World-Honored One replied,
“Because the higher fetters have been forever severed.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
How is it eternally extinguished?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Because it is ultimately severed.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"What is meant by 'tranquility'?
The World-Honored One replied,
"It is because craving for future bitter fruits has been eternally severed."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
In what way do they vanish?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"Because craving for the present fruit of suffering has been permanently severed.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
What is right view?
The World-Honored One replied:

That is to say: the wisdom of the preliminary means for clear realization (*abhisamaya*), the wisdom of the actual clear realization, and the wisdom subsequently attained after clear realization; these transcend all erroneous modes of practice based on the scriptural teachings regarding the means for knowing the objects of knowledge.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
What is right reflection?"
The Blessed One replied:

"It means that, having attained verified clarity regarding the Three Jewels as one's basis, one contemplates and recollects their qualities, thereby transcending reliance upon non-Buddhist teachers and the like."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
what is right speech?”
The World-Honored One replied:

"It refers to the untainted precepts cherished by the noble ones, which arise simultaneously with untainted mental attention; through these, one is able to correctly abstain from the four types of vocal karma and transcend all perilous and evil destinies."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
what is right action?”
The World-Honored One replied:

"It refers to the untainted precepts cherished by the noble ones, which arise simultaneously with untainted mental attention; through these, one is able to correctly distance oneself from the three types of bodily action and transcend all perilous and evil realms."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
What is right livelihood?”
The Blessed One replied:

"It refers to the untainted ethical discipline cherished by the noble ones, which arises simultaneously with untainted mental attention; it is the ability to correctly distance oneself from the two types of action—body and speech—that lead toward wrong livelihood, thereby transcending all perilous and evil destinies."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
What is right effort?”
The World-Honored One said:
"Relying upon the aspiration for the higher liberations, one arouses diligent effort to distance oneself from obstacles and bring the remedies to full completion."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One,
what is right mindfulness?"
The Blessed One said:

“The yogācāras who diligently cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā rely upon three characteristics; from time to time, within those three characteristics and through heedfulness, they maintain clear mental registration regarding the objects of practice, thereby transcending and distancing themselves from the preparatory application of the path.”
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
What is right concentration?"
The Blessed One replied:

"It means that by means of these seven factors of concentration, one supports and adorns one-pointedness of mind, and even serves as the basis for such sevenfold superior progress, as well as the basis for the elicitation of sublime qualities."
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One!

Since all the factors of enlightenment, such as the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth, are subsumed within the Noble Path, for what reason do you speak only of the eight branches of the Noble Path as the Truth of the Path?”
The Blessed One said:
"These aforementioned eight branches of the noble path universally encompass all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
He further said:
“World-Honored One!
Within the Truth of Suffering there are four aspects (*ākāra*). What is the first, called the aspect of impermanence (*anityatā-ākāra*)?
“It refers to the aspect of correct contemplation regarding the nature of arising and ceasing within the Truth of Suffering.”
"What is the second called the aspect of practicing asceticism?

It refers to taking the nature of arising and ceasing as the basis regarding the Truth of Suffering, and correctly contemplating the aspect of practice in accordance with the nature of the three types of suffering that follow."
“What is the third, called the aspect of emptiness?
It refers to the correct contemplation of the aspect of formations as being devoid of a real self-nature within the Truth of Suffering.
What is the fourth, the aspect of non-self?”
"It refers to the aspect of correct contemplation regarding the characteristic of non-self within the Truth of Suffering.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
Within the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), there are four aspects (*ākāra*). What is the first, called the aspect of cause (*hetu-ākāra*)?
It refers to the aspect of correct contemplation directed toward craving (*tṛṣṇā*), which is the causal condition for planting the seeds of all forms of suffering.
"What is the second, called the aspect of origination (*samudaya*)?
It is the correct contemplation of the aspect of conditioned phenomena within craving, which is the cause for the continuity [of existence].
What is the third, called the aspect of arising (*jāti*)?"

"It refers to correctly contemplating the characteristics of the process [of craving] within the craving that serves as the causal condition for birth in the various distinctions of the five destinies.
"What is the fourth, called the characteristic of the object-condition?"
"It means correctly observing the mode of activity within craving, which acts as a productive cause by inducing other conditions.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
Within the Truth of Cessation there are four aspects (*ākāra*). What is the first, called the aspect of cessation (*nirodha-ākāra*)?
It refers to the correct contemplation of the aspect within the cessation that is the permanent abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
“What is the second, called the aspect of peaceful conduct?
It refers to correctly contemplating the aspect of conduct within the peace of the permanent cessation of all suffering.
What is the third, called the aspect of sublime conduct?”
"It refers to correctly contemplating the mode of activity within the state of permanent abandonment, which is blameless, pure, and blissful.
"What is the fourth, called the mode of activity of detachment?"
"It refers to correctly contemplating the mode of activity within the state of permanence that is eternal cessation.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
Within the Truth of the Path, there are four aspects. What is the first, called the aspect of the path?
It refers to the aspect of correct contemplation characterized by non-erroneousness in its correspondence with the object within the Noble Path.
“What is the second called the aspect of practicing as such?
It refers to the aspect of correctly contemplating the nature of the noble path, which is forever transcendent from the world and free from all outflows.”
“What is the third called the characteristic of practicing the practice?
It refers to the characteristic of correct contemplation regarding that which has been traversed by successive noble ones throughout the past and future within the Noble Path.”
“What is the fourth, called the aspect of proceeding?
It refers to correctly contemplating the aspect of practice within the unsurpassed nature of the noble path.
He spoke again:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason are there only four noble truths?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Because these Four Noble Truths universally encompass all distinctions between the causes and effects of affliction and purification.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason are the Four Noble Truths taught in this specific order?
The World-Honored One replied,
"Because they correspond to the analogies of the world's various illnesses, the causes of illness, the cessation of illness, and the excellent medicine."
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
When entering the path of seeing, does one realize these four truths all at once?"
"Is it gradual realization?
The Blessed One replied,
"There is a distinct principle called sudden realization, and there is a distinct principle called gradual realization."
What is the distinct principle termed "simultaneous realization" (*sakṛt-abhisamaya*)?

It refers to the noble wisdom that internally realizes the true truths; because it takes as its object the non-conceptually-constructed (*apratiṣṭhita*) meaning of the realm of true wisdom through its general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it is called simultaneous realization.
What is the distinct principle called "gradual clear realization" (*anupūrvābhisamaya*)?

It refers to the knowledge of the beginner (*ādikarmika-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which observe specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the characteristics of cause and effect. Because they take these distinct characteristics as their objects through the mode of activity (*ākāra*), it is called gradual clear realization.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
If there are these four noble truths, for what reason does the World-Honored One further speak of two truths, namely, conventional truth and ultimate truth?"
The Blessed One replied:
"Within these very Four Noble Truths, whatever is the objective domain of the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya)."

"If that which is the objective domain of the wisdom realizing the most excellent ultimate truth through one's own internal realization, and which is the objective domain of non-conceptualizing wisdom, is called the ultimate truth.
He further said:
"World-Honored One!"
"These Four Noble Truths are truths for both the noble and the non-noble; for what reason does the Tathāgata speak only of 'Noble Truths'?
The World-Honored One replied:

"Regarding these Four Truths, for those who are not noble, they are called 'truths' solely by way of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); they are not called 'truths' because of a definitive conviction born of correct wisdom."
Regarding the noble ones, these are called "truths" both by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) and because they are ascertained through right knowledge and faith;
therefore, the Tathāgata teaches that there are only four kinds, which are termed the Noble Truths.
He spoke again:
"World-Honored One!
With what as its object does the sublime wisdom of the entirely complete and immeasurable dharma-realm take its support?"
"What are their modes of activity?
What are their undertakings?
The World-Honored One replied:

"This wisdom also takes these same four truths as its objects; setting aside the conceptualization of the characteristics of the truths, it enters into the modes of activity of all aspects of the truths, and proceeds toward the modes of activity that accomplish every benefit for sentient beings."
The sublime wisdom of the partially limited dharma-realm is such that, for the śrāvakas, there is no aspect of turning away from or abandoning the performance of all benefits for sentient beings;
whereas for the pratyekabuddhas, there is an aspect of turning away from the performance of all benefits for sentient beings.

The sublime wisdom of the entire, immeasurable realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) performs the activity of serving as the basis for liberation from both the afflictive and cognitive obstructions; it further performs the activity of serving as the basis for realizing the utterly pure realm of phenomena that is omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*); and it performs the activity of serving as the basis for rescuing all sentient beings from every form of calamity and affliction. This is called the excellence of the antidote to ignorance.
When the Blessed One had finished speaking this sutra, the assembly of bhikṣus silently comprehended it, rejoicing from the depths of their hearts and marveling at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Having heard what the Buddha taught, they were all filled with great joy, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of the Initial Excellence of the Analysis of Dependent Origination, Scroll II.
